extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students, writers, and researchers interested in the definition and classification of speculative fiction
extracted.subtask_description: Define and classify the umbrella genre 'speculative fiction', explain how it differs from realistic fiction, describe its purposes and historical usage, and enumerate/characterize its principal subgenres and hybrids.

rubrics_metrics.name: Speculative fiction (core definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: An umbrella genre of fiction that encompasses all the subgenres that depart from realism, or strictly imitating everyday reality, instead presenting fantastical, supernatural, futuristic, or other highly imaginative realms or beings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This catch-all genre includes, but is not limited to: fantasy, science fiction, science fantasy, superhero, paranormal and supernatural horror, alternate history, magical realism, slipstream, weird fiction, utopia and dystopia, apocalyptic and post-apocalyptic fiction. The term applies to works of literature, film, television, drama, video games, radio, and hybrid media.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree of adherence to plausibility (speculative vs realistic fiction)
rubrics_metrics.description: The umbrella genre of speculative fiction is characterized by a lesser degree of adherence to plausible depictions of individuals, events, or places, while the umbrella genre of realistic fiction is characterized by a greater degree of adherence to such depictions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Speculative fiction may depict an entirely imaginary universe or one in which the laws of nature do not strictly apply (fantasy), or impossible technology/technology beyond current understanding (science fiction), or historical moments that have concluded in imaginary ways (alternate history). Realistic fiction has settings and events that could plausibly occur in the real world.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internally consistent worldbuilding (suppositional fiction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Suppositional fiction designates fiction in which characters and stories are constrained by an internally consistent world, but not necessarily one defined by any particular genre.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasizes internal consistency of rules and consequences even when those rules differ from real-world laws; holds across speculative subgenres as a mark of coherent speculative storytelling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of 'speculative fiction' as broader/imaginative label
rubrics_metrics.description: The term 'speculative fiction' is used by some critics and writers who oppose a perceived limitation of science fiction: the requirement for a story to adhere to scientific principles, arguing that speculative fiction better defines an expanded, open, imaginative type of fiction than does 'genre fiction'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors may prefer the label to avoid being pigeonholed (e.g., Harlan Ellison) or to indicate 'no Martians' grounded plausibility (as Margaret Atwood sometimes implies). The term can signal literary/modernist directions or inclusion of multiple genre elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Speculative fiction as hybrid/combined genres
rubrics_metrics.description: The term is also used to describe genres combined into a single narrative or fictional world, such as 'science fiction, horror, fantasy...[and]...mystery'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize and allow for genre-mixing; classification should permit multiple overlapping genre elements and cross-genre storytelling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role and social function of speculative fiction
rubrics_metrics.description: In the broadest sense, the genre's concept captures both conscious and unconscious aspects of human psychology in making sense of the world, and it responds to the world by creating imaginative, inventive, and artistic expressions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such expressions can contribute to societal progress through interpersonal influences; social and cultural movements; scientific research and advances; and the philosophy of science. Historical and cultural context can be an evaluative dimension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fantasy (subgenre inclusion criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Fantasy includes elements and beings originating from or inspired by traditional stories, such as mythical creatures (dragons, elves, dwarves and fairies), magic, witchcraft, and potions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Works that foreground mythic motifs, magical systems, and creatures from folklore or invented mythologies are classed as fantasy. Examples: The Lord of the Rings, A Song of Ice and Fire, The Witcher.

rubrics_metrics.name: Science fiction (subgenre inclusion criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Science fiction features technologies and other elements that do not actually exist, but may be imagined as being created or discovered in the future through scientific advancement, such as advanced robots, interstellar travel, aliens, time travel, mutants and cyborgs. Many science fiction stories are set in the future.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inclusion typically requires speculative technological/scientific premises; stories grounded in imagined science or its societal effects fit here. Examples: 2001: A Space Odyssey, The Three-Body Problem, Star Trek.

rubrics_metrics.name: Science fantasy (hybrid subgenre)
rubrics_metrics.description: A hybrid genre that draws on or combines tropes and elements from both science fiction and fantasy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Works that mix advanced technology and scientific framing with magic/mythic elements (e.g., Dune, Star Wars) fall under this label.

rubrics_metrics.name: Superhero (subgenre inclusion criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Centers on superheroes (i.e., heroes with extraordinary abilities or powers) and their fight against evil forces such as supervillains. Typically incorporates elements of science fiction or fantasy, and may be a subgenre of these.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stories that focus on costumed/extraordinary-powered protagonists and their moral/political conflicts are categorized as superhero fiction. Examples: Marvel, DC universes, My Hero Academia.

rubrics_metrics.name: Space Western (hybrid subgenre)
rubrics_metrics.description: A hybrid genre that draws on or combines tropes and elements from both science fiction and the Western genre.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for frontier motifs transposed into space settings (e.g., Firefly, The Mandalorian).

rubrics_metrics.name: Weird West (hybrid subgenre)
rubrics_metrics.description: Also known as Weird Western—the hybrid genres of fantasy Western, horror Western and science fiction Western, combining elements of the Western genre with those of fantasy, horror and science fiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluative criterion: presence of Western setting/tones plus speculative elements from other genres (e.g., Jonah Hex, Westworld).

rubrics_metrics.name: Supernatural (subgenre inclusion criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Similar to horror and fantasy, this genre overlaps with Paranormal Romance, Contemporary Fantasy, Urban Fantasy, Occult Detective Fiction, and Paranormal Fiction. It exploits or requires plot devices or themes that often contradict commonplace, materialist assumptions about the natural world.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify works that center on supernatural phenomena that defy materialist explanations; often overlaps with other subgenres (e.g., Buffy the Vampire Slayer, Harry Potter).

rubrics_metrics.name: Horror (subgenre inclusion criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Focuses on stories that inspire fear. Villains may be either supernatural entities, such as monsters, vampires, ghosts and demons, or mundane people, such as psychopathic and cruel murderers. Often features violence and death.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Primary evaluative dimension is the aim to elicit fear, dread, or horror; includes psychological and visceral modes. Examples: Dracula, The Exorcist, Cthulhu Mythos.

rubrics_metrics.name: Utopian (subgenre inclusion criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Takes place in a highly desirable society, often presented as advanced, happy, intelligent, or even perfect and problem-free.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Works that depict intentionally idealized societies or social blueprints are utopian; can be evaluated on plausibility, critique, and satirical intent (e.g., Island, Ecotopia).

rubrics_metrics.name: Dystopian (subgenre inclusion criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Takes place in a highly undesirable society, often troubled by strict control, violence, chaos, brainwashing, or other negative elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate dystopias by the mechanisms of control and social critique they enact. Examples: 1984, The Handmaid's Tale, The Hunger Games.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternate history (subgenre inclusion criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Focuses on historical events as if they had occurred differently, and the resulting implications for the present.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion: divergence point from recorded history and plausibly developed consequences; examples include The Man in the High Castle and The Guns of the South.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apocalyptic (subgenre inclusion criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Takes place before and during a global catastrophe, typically a large-scale pandemic, natural disaster, or nuclear holocaust.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate on depiction of catastrophe onset and societal collapse; examples: On the Beach, The Day After Tomorrow, Bird Box.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-apocalyptic (subgenre inclusion criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Focuses on groups of survivors after global disasters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for narratives centered on survival, reconstruction, and changed social orders after catastrophic events. Examples: Mad Max, The Walking Dead, The Last of Us.

rubrics_metrics.name: Speculative evolution (subgenre inclusion criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Focuses on a hypothetical alternative or future evolution of humans and/or animals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Works that extrapolate biological evolution to imagine different anatomies, ecologies, or intelligences (e.g., After Man, All Tomorrows).

rubrics_metrics.name: Xenofiction (subgenre inclusion criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Follows the perspectives of non-human characters, focusing on the way their species impacts their lifestyle and thoughts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion: narrative viewpoint primarily from non-human species and exploration of alien cognition or animal perspective (e.g., Watership Down).
